The importance of chirality and the challenge of obtaining a single enantiomer

Chiral⁶⁻⁷ compounds are very important in living systems; all organisms are created from chiral building blocks and many biological processes only occur with a specific enantiomer of a molecule.  For example, the nucleosides in DNA—the fundamental genetic materials—and the amino acids that make up the proteins in our body are all chiral. Hence, a majority of modern medicines must be enantiomerically pure to work correctly without causing adverse side effects.  While the proportion of drugs that are active only as chiral compounds is increasing each year, these compounds are not easy to obtain.  Often, a chiral resolution process must be performed on a racemic mixture to isolate one isomer, or expensive chiral building blocks and/or chiral catalysts (i.e., asymmetric catalysis) must be used in the manufacture of a chirally pure compounds, which can result in higher costs for consumers.⁸

A novel solution to the aforementioned problem is to carry out syntheses in recyclable chiral solvents, where the chirality of the solvent may influence the chirality of the products due to their close proximity during the reaction.  For this application, chiral ionic liquids (CILs), ionic liquids made from chirally pure precursors,⁹ are ideal candidates.  As such, several reports have appeared in recent years on the syntheses and applications of CILs, and promising success has been achieved for asymmetric catalysis in a CIL phase.¹⁰  For instance, Malhotra and Wang described a CIL based on α-pinene and demonstrated that the achiral catalyst Cu(OSO₂CF₃)₂ dissolved in this CIL can afford enantiomeric excess (ee) of up to 76% in the diethylzinc addition to enones.¹¹

Herein, we report several new CILs and proto-CILs (i.e., organic salts that can be modified slightly to obtain CILs) that are derived from hydroquinine, a naturally occurring chiral alkaloid.  We chose hydroquinine as a precursor because it is readily available and its stereospecific structure can be effective when used for asymmetric catalysis upon modification to a CIL.  In addition, the hydroquinine structure can be modified at several sites to give a wide range of different CILs for use as asymmetry-inducing solvents in catalytic systems.

Results and Discussion
Alkylation of Hydroquinine

Alkylation of hydroquinine to the alkylammonium salt was accomplished by a simple quarternization of the tertiary amine with alkyl halides (Scheme 1).  Two different alkyl halides, n-butyl bromide and n-octyl iodide, were employed to yield compounds 1 and 4 respectively.  To drive these syntheses to completion, they were carried out under reflux in toluene.  As our initial attempt to use n-octyl bromide was not successful, the more reactive alkyl iodide was used and a longer reaction time was applied. The products were isolated by either a simple filtration (for the butyl salt) or evaporation of the solvent (for the octyl salt) and were characterized by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectrometry.
Ion Exchange

To produce compounds 2 and 3, we carried out ion exchange reactions on compound 1 using silver triflate and silver (L)-lactate, respectively (Scheme 2).  We choose L-(+)-lactate to evaluate possible chiral reinforcement between it and the hydroquinine cation.  As triflate is a non-coordinating anion, its use in ILs designed for catalysis can help ascertain the effect of potentially coordinating anions such as halides and carboxylates.
